# Design decisions and the principle behind them {#sec-principled-decisions}

**Every architectural decision in ISLA was made by one rule: an accuracy
gain is not accepted when it is known to come from a violation of a
physical principle.** A surrogate for a boundary-value problem should depend
on the geometry, the boundary conditions and the physics, and on nothing
else. When a change improves the score by reading the mesher's cell pattern,
the sampling density, or a statistic of the drawn sample, the improvement is
a fit to the discretization, and it will not survive a different mesher, a
different sampling law, or a geometry the training set did not contain. This
appendix is the ledger of every decision of that kind: the alternative it
rejected, what the alternative would have bought on the in-distribution
metric, what it consumed that the physics does not provide, and the evidence.
It exists so that the paper on ISLA can say *why* the architecture is what it
is, and so that the position is stated plainly for others: a program that
wants highly generalizable physics surrogates has to be willing to leave
measured accuracy on the table when that accuracy is known to be
non-physical.^[Not everything that is measured counts, and not everything
that counts can be measured. The aphorism is William Bruce Cameron's
(*Informal Sociology*, 1963); it is often misattributed to Einstein.]

## The criterion, and how it was audited {#sec-principled-criterion}

**The operational form of the principle is consistency in the fine-mesh
limit: a prediction that converges to one field under refinement and to the
same field under two sampling laws** (@sec-principle). A dependence on the
sampling distribution that does not vanish with refinement is a defect,
however much it improves a score at a fixed cell count. A falling error with
more cells is not a defect. A different answer under a different sampler at
every count is. The test that decides is therefore never a single accuracy
number: it is the consistency benchmark of @sec-consistency-bench, which
scores every model under three samplers at four cell counts, and its
training-law twin (@sec-training-law), which trains every model under two
sampling laws and scores both on one independent draw.

Two questions are asked of every proposed change, before and after it is
measured. *Why should this work*, in mechanistic terms? And would a
practitioner of classical CFD look at the construction without objecting to
what it consumes? Changes that cannot answer both are run, when they are
run at all, as ablations, and are labeled so wherever they appear. The same
two questions are the reason ISLA has one configuration: the weights-off
ablation is not adopted on the rungs where it scores better, and no frame
that centers on a statistic of the sample is in the class
(@sec-nb-principle-redirect, @sec-nb-frame-cleanup).

## The ledger {#sec-principled-ledger}

**Each row names the decision as it stands in ISLA, the alternative it
rejected, and what the alternative would have cost the physics.** "What it
would have bought" is the alternative's gain on the in-distribution
surface-pressure metric (float32, seed means) where it had one, with the
cell budget it was measured at; "what it reads" is the non-physical quantity
the gain came from; the evidence column points to the chapter or notebook
entry that carries the numbers and their artifacts. Two rows are decisions
of protocol and code rather than of architecture, and one is in progress;
each says so.

: The design-decision ledger. Every number is stated in the chapter or notebook entry the row points to and carries its artifact there. How to read this: a row records what the rejected alternative would have bought *in distribution* and what it would have read; it does not rank the decisions by size, and a row whose gain column says "nothing" is a decision made on principle with no accuracy at stake. The cosine-routing row is a decision in progress and the default has not changed. {#tbl-principled-ledger}

**Two rows deserve a sentence each, because they are the ones where the
principle cost the most.**

**The measure weights** are the clearest case. With them, a slice state is
a quadrature estimate of a surface integral; without them it is a mean over
whichever points the mesher happened to place, and the network learns the
mesher. The price on the wings is real and understood: part of it is the
estimator variance of a quadrature-weighted mean over a heavy-tailed draw of
cell areas, which shrinks with cell count and is nearly gone at 40,000 cells
on the cars; the rest is mesh-pattern content in the ablation, which does
not shrink and which collapses the moment the sampling law changes. An
accuracy table at one cell count cannot tell these apart. The consistency
benchmark can, and it decided.

**The frame** is the case where the trade was closest, and it is stated
without softening. Where the same wings recur between training and
validation, an estimated center and scale are worth 3 to 9% at the
exploration budget against the origin-free construction, and at 210
recurring cases the similarity-gauge variant (removed) met the accuracy
condition this program had set for accepting it. It is not in the class,
because the rungs that test geometries the model has never seen favor the
origin-free construction, because on DrivAerML at 435 cars the variant is
within seed noise of ISLA (the price of not being told the body's center is
at most about 2%; @sec-nb-sgref-verdict), and because an estimated frame is
a statistic of the sample even when it is a consistent one. For a fixed
fleet of shapes an estimated frame is the better instrument; ISLA is built
for the shapes that have not been seen yet.

## What we would ask of the field {#sec-principled-ask}

**Three practices follow from the ledger, and none of them is expensive.**

- **Measure consistency, not only accuracy.** Score every model under at
  least two sampling laws and at more than one cell count, and report
  whether the answers converge to each other; then train under a second law
  and score on the first. A model that is 10% better at 10,000 cells and
  10x worse under a different sampler, or 8x worse when trained under a
  different law, has learned the mesher (@sec-consistency-bench,
  @sec-training-law).
- **Locate every gain before adopting it.** When a change improves the
  score, run the test that would reveal a discretization dependence, and ask
  what the change consumes that the physics does not supply. A mechanism that
  cannot be stated is a hypothesis; a gain whose mechanism is the mesh is not
  a gain.
- **Preregister the bar and keep the refuted configurations runnable.**
  Every decision above was made against a bar written before the run. The
  class ISLA ships carries one frame and the options the chapters compare
  against as labeled ablations (the weights-off ablation, the interior
  decodes, both routing forms); the rejected frames (the legacy centered
  variant and the similarity-gauge variant), the constant reference length
  and the diagnostic options are not in the class and their checkpoints do
  not load, and they remain runnable, with their tests, only at the git tag
  `isla-research-full`, so that the price can be re-measured when the data
  or the metric change (@sec-nb-frame-cleanup, @sec-program-status).

The accuracy metric is one number about one discretization of one dataset.
It is necessary and it is not sufficient, and a research program that
optimizes it alone will converge on surrogates that know their mesher better
than their physics.
